lesson.title: The Open Standard Inside the Network: How OSPF Routes Within a Domain
lesson.summary: OSPF is the open, standardized link state protocol that most real networks use to route traffic within a single administratively controlled domain.
lesson.body:
Link state routing and Dijkstra's algorithm describe a strategy; OSPF, which stands for Open Shortest Path First, is the real protocol that implements that strategy inside most production networks today. OSPF is what is called an interior gateway protocol, meaning it is designed to run within a single administratively controlled network, such as a company's internal network or the internal backbone of an internet service provider, rather than between independent organizations.

The word "open" in OSPF's name is a deliberate contrast with older proprietary alternatives. OSPF is a fully public, vendor neutral standard, published and maintained through the Internet Engineering Task Force's RFC process, with OSPF version 2, the version used for IPv4, specified in RFC 2328. That means any vendor can implement it and any network operator can read exactly how it is supposed to behave, rather than trusting a single company's closed implementation. That openness is a large part of why OSPF became the dominant interior routing protocol across the industry.

Mechanically, OSPF is link state routing exactly as described earlier, applied concretely. Each OSPF router discovers its neighbors, measures or is configured with a cost for each link, by default derived from the link's bandwidth so faster links look cheaper, and packages this into link state advertisements that are reliably flooded to every other router in the same OSPF domain. Every router ends up with an identical link state database describing the full internal topology, and every router independently runs Dijkstra's algorithm rooted at itself to build its own shortest path tree, from which it derives its forwarding table.

One practical feature OSPF adds on top of the bare link state idea is areas. A very large network flooding every link state change to every single router can become a real scalability burden, so OSPF allows an administrator to partition the network into areas, with a mandatory backbone area, called area zero, that every other area must connect through. Routers only flood full topology detail within their own area, and between areas only summarized reachability information crosses, which keeps the link state database and the Dijkstra computation manageable even in large networks, while still preserving the core link state guarantee within each area. OSPF also supports equal cost multipath, meaning if two paths to a destination happen to have identical total cost, traffic can be spread across both rather than arbitrarily picking one.
